title: Quantization safeguards & runtime layer-probing: KV warmup and onprem fallback review
summary: Redwood and Heliox discussed a plan to triage accuracy regressions observed after AWQ/GPTQ quantization. Primary focus: layer-probing to find sensitive layers, KV cache warmup/staleness interaction with batching, and an on-prem VPC fallback plan with KMS and audit requirements. Agreed next steps: run a layerwise sensitivity sweep, share security docs, and schedule a 2-hour on-prem benchmark next week.
action_items: Ethan Brooks: run layerwise sensitivity sweep for Heliox's 7B model with AWQ profile and produce per-layer delta table (due: 2028-01-22)
Diego Marquez: provide sample request traces and p99 latency windows for the last 2 weeks (due: 2028-01-18)
Maya Patel: share onboarding / security packet (SOC2 docs, KMS integration notes, audit log exports) and benchmark sheet link (due: 2028-01-17)
next_steps: Schedule 2-hour on-prem benchmark in Heliox staging (tentative: 2028-01-20)
Ethan to upload AWQ vs GPTQ activations snapshot to shared benchmark spreadsheet
Team to test KV cache warmup toggles (prefill vs lazy warm) in canary and report regressions
transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-01-15 16:00 UTC | Duration 62m | Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Brooks (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Heliox), Diego Marquez (Heliox), Priya Sharma (Heliox CTO)

[00:00:05] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll kick off in a sec, uh quick check audio — can you hear me okay?
[00:00:10] Aisha: yep loud and clear, thanks Maya.
[00:00:20] Maya: great. quick agenda: the accuracy regression you saw after AWQ conversion, go over layer-probing plan, discuss KV cache warmup and batching interactions, and then onprem/VPC fallback requirements. Ethan is gonna drive the tech bits.
[00:00:38] Ethan: cool, i'll start with what we observed. so from your notes, the post-quantize rollout had a ~2.8% drop on your qa eval set, right? there were also intermittent p99 latency spikes when batching hit 8-12 requests.
[00:00:55] Diego: yeah that's right, the regression is most visible on instruction-following tasks — multiple choice and code-gen are fine-ish. latency spikes happen when KV lookups are colder.
[00:01:10] Priya: just to add, we run in a VPC on prem, strict KMS controls, can't ship raw activations off-site. we need a fallback that doesn't violate that.
[00:01:25] Ethan: noted. two threads then: accuracy root-cause (layer sensitivity vs quant noise) and runtime behavior (KV cache staleness + batching). i'll cover the layer probes first.
[00:01:40] Ethan: methodology we propose is layerwise perturbation: quantize per-layer (or dequantize single layers) to see where the delta spikes. we do an AWQ pass and also a GPTQ-style pass to compare. importantly, watch for distribution shifts in the attention keys/vals.
[00:01:58] Aisha: quick q — when you say GPTQ pass, do you mean full retrain calibration or the fast-blockwise method we've used? some of our model ops prefer the faster route.
[00:02:12] Ethan: good question. we'll run both: the fast blockwise (cheap) and one GPTQ calibration for suspicious layers. fast run gives a signal, GPTQ is the confirm. sometimes the fast route misses subtle bias drift.
[00:02:30] Maya: and we'll capture logits/softmax divergences, not just token-level accuracy, to see distribution shifts.
[00:02:40] Diego: for the runtime side, we saw that when KV cache is cold, the first few tokens per session are slower and sometimes have more hallucinations — is that expected?
[00:02:52] Ethan: yes. two interactions: KV cache warmup affects how subsequent tokens attend — if prefill is incomplete or if the cache has staleness (we saw a bug in earlier runtime where stale segments were reused), then quantized kernels can amplify small errors. the batching heuristic also delays cache writes in some backends.
[00:03:15] Aisha: can you explain the 'amplify' part — is that numeric noise in INT8 AWQ or memory layout differences?
[00:03:24] Ethan: mostly quant noise — AWQ's asymmetric weights can shift activation magnitudes. if attention latents are near quant boundaries, the rounding can flip token selection probabilities. in a warmed cache those errors are damped by context; in cold they surface.
[00:03:44] Maya: (interrupting) and this is where layer-probing helps us find which attention or MLP layers are sensitive. you may find top-2 layers contribute 80% of the delta.
[00:03:55] Priya: fine, but operationally, we need an on-prem fallback plan. if a canary shows >1.5% regression, how do we automatically route traffic to a higher-precision fallback within the VPC without leaking data?
[00:04:10] Ethan: two options: 1) in-process precision mixing — keep the critical layers in FP16/FP32 while rest are AWQ. that's a thin change and runs on same machine, or 2) fallback route to a dedicated higher-precision pool in your onprem cluster. both stay within VPC and respect KMS because no data leaves the network.
[00:04:30] Diego: option 1 sounds better for latency but might cost more compute. option 2 requires orchestrating routing and capacity.
[00:04:38] Maya: yep tradeoff: compute vs complexity. we can start with a layer-gating canary to minimize perf hit.
[00:04:46] Ethan: about batching — we noticed your default batch window is 30ms. when batch grows to enable higher throughput, the effective per-request latency p99 goes up and the cache write ordering shifts. We recommend a dynamic batch-size cap and early KV flush for low-latency flows.
[00:05:05] Diego: is that something Redwood runtime can do automatically? we've been tweaking heuristics in our own stack.
[00:05:12] Ethan: yes, we have a policy engine: you can set route-level SLOs, e.g., max-latency 120ms p99, and runtime adjusts batching thresholds and can force immediate cache commits for those routes. we'll share the policy snippet.
[00:05:28] Aisha: what about seed/repro issues — we've seen non-deterministic diffs across runs after quantizing.
[00:05:36] Ethan: two separate causes: RNG seed for attention dropout (if used), and non-deterministic kernel scheduling on different GPU drivers. with quant we also saw reduced numerical stability that magnifies small nondet differences. solution: fix seeds, use deterministic kernels where possible, and run the layer-probing with multiple seeds to average out noise.
[00:05:58] Maya: we'll add an entry to the bug/triage doc: 'run with 3 seeds at minimum for layer probes'.
[00:06:05] Priya: security question — we require KMS signing of model binaries and audit logs for any fallback events. can Redwood produce signed artifacts and event logs accessible via our SIEM?
[00:06:18] Maya: yes — we support customer KMS via your HSM and can push audit logs to your syslog/S3 endpoint. Ethan will include the exact fields we emit.
[00:06:28] Ethan: fields: timestamp, model_id, variant, routed_pool, fallback_trigger, raw_delta_metric (we can obfuscate inputs per your policy).
[00:06:40] Diego: that should be fine, just need field mapping so our SIEM can parse.
[00:06:45] Ethan: we'll send a sample JSON schema.
[00:06:49] -- 10 minutes of technical walkthrough slides shared --
[00:16:55] Ethan: demo note: when we ran AWQ on 7B in our env we saw layer 10 and 22 driving 65% of logit divergence. GPTQ calibration on layer 22 recovered ~1.6% of the loss. However on your dataset the same layers might differ.
[00:17:15] Aisha: so the approach is: run cheap per-layer quant checks, then selectively GPTQ-calibrate top N layers? that aligns with our ops budget.
[00:17:24] Ethan: exactly. cheap scan -> GPTQ for top 3 layers -> mixed-precision deploy.
[00:17:30] Priya: any known pathology with FP8? we were considering trying FP8 on hot routes.
[00:17:37] Ethan: FP8 can provide better dynamic range in some MLPs but it's less mature in our kernels and driver stacks. plus FP8 runtime ops currently have variable perf across GPU families; in some cases INT8 AWQ is more predictable. I'd treat FP8 as experimental for now.
[00:17:55] Diego: we'd like perf numbers: raw throughput, token/s, and cost delta.
[00:18:02] Maya: we'll attach the benchmark sheet, it has a matrix per GPU SKU, per precision. link: redwood.ai/bench/heliox-int-bench (note: internal link).
[00:18:12] Ethan: back to KV warmup: two quick toggles to test in canary — prefill cache on session start with recent context, or use lazy warm but enable early write-through so first real write is durable. Prefill reduces first-token variance but costs extra memory.
[00:18:30] Aisha: memory is less of a concern, latency is the big one. prefill seems attractive.
[00:18:36] Ethan: ok we'll test both toggles. also watch for staleness windows when you have many concurrent sessions — our runtime's KV eviction defaults to LRU, which can evict useful segments if not tuned.
[00:18:50] Diego: we did see cold cache churn at 2k concurrency on our cluster.
[00:18:55] Ethan: then bumping max-kv-size and switching to affinity-based sharding might help. we'll propose numbers after we see traces.
[00:19:06] -- timestamps jump, mid-call Q&A and small interruptions --
[00:31:05] Aisha: practical question — how long does the layer-probing sweep take? we have a 7B fleet, 10k eval samples.
[00:31:14] Ethan: fast blockwise sweep is about 30-60 minutes per pass on a 4-GPU rig for 10k samples. GPTQ calibrations add another 1-2 hours per calibrated layer. we can parallelize across cluster nodes.
[00:31:30] Priya: ok, budget for a day of runs then.
[00:31:34] Maya: we recommend running the fast sweep first and then prioritizing based on the delta table.
[00:31:40] Diego: one more nuance — after some quant conversions we observed token-prob skews only on longer contexts (>1024). any thoughts?
[00:31:50] Ethan: yes, longer context increases accumulation of small numeric errors and also stresses KV cache coherency. quant rounding at early layers can produce different key distributions causing downstream attention shifts after many tokens. it's why we look at long-context evals too.
[00:32:05] Aisha: can Redwood runtime simulate long-run sessions with realistic user patterns?
[00:32:10] Ethan: yes, we have a workload replay harness. Diego can send traces and we'll run long-context stress tests.
[00:32:18] Diego: will do.
[00:32:22] -- later: operational runbook & failover discussion --
[00:45:05] Maya: for the runbook: detection -> classify (accuracy vs perf) -> remediation. detection rule example: rolling 1k inference window, trigger if delta >1.2% or p99 latency > SLO. classification is automated by our eval harness. remediation: layered approach: 1) real-time routing to mixed-precision, 2) if persistent, rollback to previous model variant, 3) if perf issue, adjust batching/kv policies.
[00:45:35] Priya: can we get an API call to flip a route to mixed-precision inside our VPC? we want RBAC so only ops can trigger.
[00:45:44] Maya: yes, RBAC control via SSO groups, and audit log for each change.
[00:45:50] Aisha: any gotchas with model-signing and canary artifacts?
[00:45:55] Ethan: we produce signed model manifests and can keep signed rollback images. onprem may require you to mirror artifacts into your registry, which we support via signed tarballs that your KMS signs.
[00:46:08] Diego: sounds workable.
[00:46:12] -- final 10 minutes recap and next steps --
[00:53:00] Maya: recap: Ethan will run layerwise sweep (fast pass + targeted GPTQ), Diego will send traces and latency windows, Maya will send security docs and bench link. we'll schedule the on-prem 2h bench for the 20th.
[00:53:15] Priya: agreed, and please include the sample audit log fields for our SIEM mapping.
[00:53:21] Maya: will do.
[00:53:25] Aisha: thanks all, this was helpful.
[00:53:30] Ethan: quick note — if we find a single-layer hot spot, we can usually gate that layer to FP16 with minimal perf hit. i'll quantify the expected token/sec delta in the sweep results.
[00:53:45] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with action items and timelines. meeting end.
[00:61:05] (end)

References shared in call: redwood internal bench sheet (redwood.ai/bench/heliox-int-bench), security packet (redwood.ai/security/heliox-packet), triage doc (redwood.ai/triage/quant-playbook).
Note: transcript includes occasional mis-hearings and shorthand (G P T Q vs GPTQ, A W Q vs AWQ), speaker overlaps, and filler words to reflect recording artifacts.
notes: Customer is cautious about FP8; prefers AWQ + targeted GPTQ calibration. On-prem constraints (KMS, audit) are blockers for any routing that leaves VPC. Prioritize layer-probing then canary mixed-precision.
